title: Start with what we can observe
focus: Observations, models, and a prediction we can test
figure: COLOR IT · WATCH A PATTERN FORM
example: A cart is at 2 m, 3 m, then 4 m, one second apart. Predict its position one second later.
solution: GIVEN x = 2, 3, 4 m 1 s between readings EQUATION next = last + change each second WORK change = 3 − 2 = +1 m next = 4 m + 1 m ANSWER 5 m if the motion continues the same way

words.definition: Something we record or measure, like a position at a time.
A useful “if”: if the motion keeps going the same way, we can continue the pattern.
An estimate of what comes next, made by continuing the pattern.
One that measurements can answer. “Where will it be tomorrow?” — yes. “Who should pay for a mission?” — no; that also needs human decisions.

title: Where you finish is not the whole trip
focus: Position, distance, and displacement
figure: COLOR IT · ONE TRIP, THREE QUESTIONS
example: A cart goes from 2 m to 6 m, then back to 4 m. Right is positive. Find the distance and the displacement.
solution: GIVEN x i = 2 m turn at 6 m x f = 4 m EQUATION distance = leg 1 + leg 2 Δx = x f − x i WORK 4 m + 2 m 4 m − 2 m ANSWER distance 6 m displacement +2 m

words.definition: Where are you? Measured from a chosen zero, with a chosen + direction.
How much travel? Counts every part of the path. Never negative.
What changed from start to finish? The sign gives the direction.
Distance has size only (scalar). Displacement has size and direction (vector).

title: Read motion from the slope
focus: Velocity, speed, and position-time graphs
figure: COLOR IT · READ A GRAPH AS A MOTION STORY
example: A cart goes from 8 m to 2 m in 3 s. Right is positive. Find its velocity.
solution: GIVEN x i = 8 m x f = 2 m Δt = 3 s EQUATION v = Δx ÷ Δt WORK Δx = 2 − 8 = −6 m v = −6 m ÷ 3 s ANSWER −2 m/s 2 m/s to the left

words.definition: How fast and which way. The rate position changes.
How fast only. The size of the velocity, with no direction.
Steepness of a line: rise ÷ run. On a position–time graph, slope = velocity.
Total distance ÷ time. A scalar — no direction. Velocity adds the sign.

title: Read the axes before you read the line
focus: Velocity-time graphs, signed area, and components
figure: COLOR IT · AREA COUNTS THE CHANGE
example: Velocity is +3 m/s for 2 s. Find the displacement and name its direction.
solution: GIVEN v = +3 m/s t = 2 s EQUATION Δx = v × t WORK Δx = (3 m/s)(2 s) ANSWER +6 m 6 m to the right

words.definition: The vertical axis shows velocity , not position. Read the label first.
Steady velocity — not necessarily stopped.
Height × width = displacement. Area below zero is negative displacement.
The separate east and north changes that make up one diagonal displacement.

title: Start with the starting position
focus: Steady-velocity predictions and their possible range
example: A cart starts at 8 m and moves at −2 m/s for 3 s. Where is it at the end?
solution: GIVEN x i = 8 m v = −2 m/s t = 3 s EQUATION x f = x i + v × t WORK change = (−2)(3) = −6 m x f = 8 − 6 ANSWER 2 m moved 6 m left

words.definition: Where the object is at t = 0. It is often not zero.
Velocity × time: how far the position shifts.
Start + change.
A ± bound. “10 ± 2 m” means 8 m to 12 m. More time usually means a wider range.

title: Keep direction attached to every arrow
focus: Tip-to-tail addition and splitting vectors into parts
example: A 20 N pull points 30° above the +x axis. Split it into its x and y parts.
solution: GIVEN F = 20 N θ = 30° from +x EQUATION F x = F cos θ F y = F sin θ WORK 20 cos 30° 20 sin 30° ANSWER 17.3 N, 10.0 N parts of one force, not two new forces

words.definition: A quantity with size and direction, drawn as an arrow.
Start each arrow where the last one ends. Do not turn or stretch it.
The east–west or north–south part of a vector.
The overall arrow from the first start to the final finish.

title: Acceleration means velocity is changing
focus: Reading dot patterns and calculating change each second
example: A cart’s velocity changes from 0 to 8 m/s in 4 s. Find its acceleration.
solution: GIVEN v i = 0 m/s v f = 8 m/s Δt = 4 s EQUATION a = Δv ÷ Δt WORK Δv = 8 − 0 = 8 m/s a = 8 ÷ 4 ANSWER 2 m/s² gains 2 m/s each second

words.definition: The rate velocity changes: how much velocity is gained or lost each second.
v and a have the same sign. Gaps between equal-time dots grow.
v and a have opposite signs. Braking is acceleration too.
A direction change is a velocity change, even at steady speed.

title: Choose a motion model before an equation
focus: Steady acceleration and displacement from average velocity
figure: COLOR IT · TRIANGLE OR AVERAGE: SAME AREA
example: A cart speeds up steadily from 0 to 8 m/s in 4 s. Find its displacement.
solution: GIVEN v i = 0, v f = 8 m/s t = 4 s constant a EQUATION Δx = ½(v i + v f ) × t WORK average = (0 + 8) ÷ 2 = 4 m/s Δx = 4 × 4 ANSWER +16 m average works: a is constant

words.definition: Equal gaps; velocity does not change. Use v × t.
Velocity changes by the same amount each second.
(start + final) ÷ 2 — only when acceleration is constant.
A choice with a reason: “I chose ___ because the velocity ___.”

title: Moving does not require an unbalanced force
focus: Newton's first law, balanced forces, and inertia
example: A cart rolls right, then slows down. What does that tell you about its net horizontal force?
solution: GIVEN moving right speed decreasing EQUATION a ≠ 0 → net force ≠ 0 WORK velocity changes → there is a net force; it opposes the motion ANSWER Net force left opposite the motion

words.definition: A push or pull from an interaction with another object.
The combined effect of all forces on one object.
1st law: at rest stays at rest; moving keeps its velocity — unless ΣF ≠ 0.
An object keeps its velocity unless a net force changes it. More mass, more inertia.

title: Name what is doing the pushing or pulling
focus: Force sources, contact forces, mass, and weight
example: A 3 kg object rests on a level table. Find its weight and name the force that supports it.
solution: GIVEN m = 3 kg g ≈ 10 N/kg EQUATION W = m × g WORK W = 3 × 10 = 30 N down table pushes up equally ANSWER 30 N normal force 30 N up

words.definition: Every force has a source (what pushes or pulls) and a receiver.
Normal (surface, ⟂), friction (along surface, opposes slip), tension (rope), applied (a push).
Gravity acts without touching.
Mass is amount of matter (kg). Weight is Earth’s gravitational pull (N).

title: Change the mass and watch the acceleration
focus: A fair test with the same net force
example: In one trial, velocity rises from 0 to 4 m/s in 2 s. Find the acceleration.
solution: GIVEN v i = 0 m/s v f = 4 m/s Δt = 2 s EQUATION a = Δv ÷ Δt WORK Δv = 4 − 0 = 4 m/s a = 4 ÷ 2 ANSWER 2 m/s² use your own measured graph

words.definition: Change one thing at a time.
Total system mass: cart + added masses + hanger.
Hanging mass, track, start point, release (no push).
The slope of each velocity–time graph is the acceleration.

title: Keep the mass fixed and change the force
focus: A proportional relationship and Newton's second law
example: In an ideal 2 kg system, 2 N gives 1 m/s². Predict the acceleration at 4 N with the same mass.
solution: GIVEN F = 2 N → a = 1 m/s² new F = 4 N same mass EQUATION a ∝ F (same mass) WORK 4 N ÷ 2 N = 2× the force a = 2 × 1 m/s² ANSWER 2 m/s² acceleration doubles

words.definition: The hanging weight that pulls the cart system.
Held constant: move masses from cart to hanger; never add new ones.
Double the net force → double the acceleration.
Friction lowers the net force, so real data can sit below the ideal line.

title: Find the net force before dividing by mass
focus: Using Newton's second law with opposing forces
example: A 4 kg cart has 12 N pulling right and 4 N of friction left. Find the acceleration.
solution: GIVEN m = 4 kg 12 N right 4 N left EQUATION a = F net ÷ m WORK F net = 12 − 4 = 8 N right a = 8 ÷ 4 ANSWER 2 m/s² right with the net force

words.definition: Combine opposite forces: subtract and keep the direction of the larger one.
Uses the net force, never just one pull.
Acceleration points the same way as the net force.
Net force 0 N → a = 0 m/s² (still or constant velocity).

title: A force pair belongs to two different objects
focus: Newton's third law and the receiver of each force
figure: COLOR IT · ONE INTERACTION, TWO FORCES
example: Earth pulls an apple downward. Name the third-law partner force and the object that receives it.
solution: GIVEN Earth → apple gravity, down EQUATION swap the object names WORK apple → Earth gravity, up ANSWER Apple pulls Earth up Earth receives it

words.definition: When A pushes B, B pushes A at the same time.
Same size, same type of force, opposite directions.
One force acts on A, its partner acts on B — so they never cancel.
Equal forces, different masses → different accelerations.

title: Draw only the forces on your chosen object
focus: A clear free-body diagram and balanced lamp forces
figure: COLOR IT · A BOX PULLED RIGHT
example: A 20 N lamp hangs at rest from one vertical rope. Draw and label its forces.
solution: GIVEN weight = 20 N at rest one rope EQUATION sources: Earth, rope WORK weight 20 N down tension up, balances it ANSWER Tension 20 N up equal-length arrows

words.definition: Only the forces acting on one chosen object.
Replace the object with a simple shape; draw arrows from it.
Every arrow needs one: rope, floor, table, Earth.
Motion is not an interaction. Leave velocity off the diagram.

title: Use the force diagram to find acceleration
focus: Ramp directions, weight components, and net force
figure: COLOR IT · FORCES ON A RAMP
example: A 2 kg block has a 7 N downhill weight component and 3 N of friction uphill. Find its acceleration.
solution: GIVEN m = 2 kg 7 N downhill 3 N uphill EQUATION a = F net ÷ m WORK F net = 7 − 3 = 4 N downhill a = 4 ÷ 2 ANSWER 2 m/s² downhill

words.definition: Points perpendicular to (straight away from) the surface — on a ramp, it is tilted.
Always points straight down, toward Earth.
The downhill part of weight. A way to calculate — not an extra force.
Same direction as the net force.

title: Friction adjusts before sliding begins
focus: Static friction, its limit, and kinetic friction
figure: COLOR IT · BEFORE AND DURING SLIDING
example: A 2 kg crate slides right. Pull = 10 N right; kinetic friction = 4 N left. Find its acceleration.
solution: GIVEN m = 2 kg pull 10 N right f k 4 N left EQUATION a = F net ÷ m WORK F net = 10 − 4 = 6 N right a = 6 ÷ 2 ANSWER 3 m/s² right

words.definition: Before sliding. Adjusts to match the pull, up to a limit.
The greatest static friction possible. Pull past it and sliding starts.
During sliding. Use the supplied value.
When given: kinetic friction = μ × normal force.

title: Find what is needed to make the forces balance
focus: Equilibrium and missing support forces
figure: COLOR IT · SUPPORTS MUST TOTAL THE WEIGHT
example: A 40 N sign hangs at rest from two vertical ropes. One tension is 15 N. Find the other.
solution: GIVEN weight 40 N rope 1 = 15 N at rest EQUATION up = down WORK 15 + T 2 = 40 T 2 = 40 − 15 ANSWER 25 N up

words.definition: Acceleration is zero. The forces sum to zero in every direction.
At rest or moving at constant velocity.
Whatever is needed to make each direction balance.
Zero velocity for an instant does not guarantee equilibrium.

title: Repair the reasoning, not just the answer
focus: Finding the first mistake and checking the correction
example: A 3 kg cart has 9 N right and 3 N left. A student writes 9 ÷ 3 = 3 m/s². Correct it.
solution: GIVEN m = 3 kg 9 N right 3 N left EQUATION a = F net ÷ m WORK F net = 9 − 3 = 6 N right a = 6 ÷ 3 ANSWER 2 m/s² right missed: net force first

words.definition: Trace the whole path vs. join start to finish.
Combine all forces before dividing by mass.
A minus sign is not “slow.” Compare sizes for speed.
Act on different objects, so they never cancel.

title: Connect the forces to the final position
focus: The complete chain from net force to a motion prediction
figure: COLOR IT · ONE CHAIN, FOUR LINKS
example: A cart has zero net force and already moves at +2 m/s. After 3 s, find its velocity and displacement.
solution: GIVEN F net = 0 N v = +2 m/s t = 3 s EQUATION a = 0 → v constant Δx = v × t WORK v stays +2 m/s Δx = 2 × 3 ANSWER +2 m/s, +6 m

words.definition: Net force → acceleration → velocity → position.
Gives constant acceleration: a straight v–t line.
Velocity stays the same; position still changes.
A central value with limits. Not a guarantee.

title: Make the situation clear before calculating
focus: A reference frame, useful evidence, and a prediction plan
figure: COLOR IT · MAKE THE SITUATION VISIBLE
example: Check a prediction: an object starts at 2 m and moves at a steady +3 m/s for 4 s.
solution: GIVEN x i = 2 m v = +3 m/s t = 4 s · steady v EQUATION x f = x i + v × t WORK change = 3 × 4 = +12 m x f = 2 + 12 ANSWER 14 m check: direction + size + start

words.definition: The zero everything is measured from. Mark it on your sketch.
Every value copied with its unit.
State it: steady velocity or constant acceleration.
Read the lower and upper values before making a claim.

title: Explain what the forecast means and what limits it
focus: Claim, evidence, reasoning, and a visible revision
example: Defend a prediction: a 2 kg cart under 4 N net force, from rest at 1 m, for 2 s; model bound ± 1 m.
solution: GIVEN F net = 4 N, m = 2 kg x i = 1 m, t = 2 s bound ± 1 m EQUATION force → a → v → x WORK a = 2 m/s², v = 4 m/s Δx = 4 m, x f = 5 m ANSWER 4 to 6 m assumes constant forces

words.definition: Your prediction, stated clearly.
Visible work: a graph, sketch, or calculation.
What the model leaves out or assumes.
A corrected step, shown — and how it changes later results.

title: What does the evidence let us say?
focus: Evidence, inference, models, and prediction
figure: COLOR IT · WATCH A PATTERN FORM
example: A cart is at 10 m, 8 m, and 6 m at 0, 1, and 2 s. Predict its position at 4 s, and name an observation that would challenge the model.
solution: GIVEN x = 10, 8, 6 m t = 0, 1, 2 s EQUATION new x = start + change × time WORK change = −2 m each second x (4 s) = 6 + (−2)(2) ANSWER 2 m limit: a 3 m reading would challenge it

words.definition: What was actually stated or measured. “An object is approaching.”
A conclusion that still needs testing. “It will hit Earth.”
A simplified description with stated assumptions that makes a testable prediction.
“Is it bad?” → “Will its predicted path intersect Earth’s position at the same time?”

title: One trip can have several correct descriptions
focus: Position, distance, displacement, and reference frames
figure: COLOR IT · ONE TRIP, THREE QUESTIONS
example: Start at −3 m, move to +2 m, then finish at −1 m. Find the distance and the displacement, with units.
solution: GIVEN x i = −3 m turn at +2 m x f = −1 m EQUATION distance = Σ |leg| Δ x = x f − x i WORK |2 − (−3)| + |−1 − 2| = 5 + 3 −1 − (−3) ANSWER distance 8 m displacement +2 m

words.definition: A signed coordinate in a reference frame: choose an origin and a + direction. x = −2 m is 2 m left of the origin.
Sum of the length of every leg: | x 2 − x 1 | + | x 3 − x 2 | + … Never negative.
Δ x = x f − x i . Its sign depends on the axis you chose; the physical motion does not.
A scalar has magnitude + units (distance, time). A vector also has direction (displacement).

title: A graph can tell the story of motion
focus: Average velocity, speed, and position-time graphs
figure: COLOR IT · READ A GRAPH AS A MOTION STORY
example: A straight x – t line passes through (2 s, 14 m) and (6 s, 6 m). Find the velocity, then predict x at 8 s.
solution: GIVEN (2 s, 14 m) (6 s, 6 m) predict at 8 s EQUATION v = Δ x ÷ Δ t x = x i + v t WORK v = (6 − 14) ÷ (6 − 2) x (8) = 6 + (−2)(2) ANSWER −2 m/s; 2 m if the line continues

words.definition: v̄ = Δ x ÷ Δ t . Carries direction; summarizes a whole interval.
Total distance ÷ elapsed time. No direction.
On an x – t graph, slope = velocity (units m/s). Height = position, not velocity.
Velocity at one moment: the tangent slope on a curved x – t graph.

title: Velocity tells us more than speed
focus: Signed area, displacement, and velocity components
example: A cart moves at +3 m/s for 2 s , then −1 m/s for 2 s . Find its displacement and total distance.
solution: GIVEN v 1 = +3 m/s v 2 = −1 m/s 2 s per interval EQUATION Use areas because each interval has steady v . WORK Δ x = 3(2) − 1(2) distance = 6 + 2 ANSWER +4 m ; 8 m Return travel reduces Δ x , not distance.

words.definition: Above zero adds displacement; below zero subtracts it.
Add area sizes, including the return trip.
A vector’s signed part along one axis.
Name the starting axis and turn direction.

title: A prediction should carry its uncertainty
focus: Constant velocity, bounds, and a range of possible positions
example: A cart starts at 8 ± 0.5 m and moves at −2.0 ± 0.1 m/s for an exact 3 s . Find its predicted position interval.
solution: GIVEN x 0 = 8 ± 0.5 m v = −2.0 ± 0.1 m/s t = 3 s ; steady v EQUATION Steady v : x f = x 0 + vt . Add input bounds. WORK x f = 8 − 2(3) δ x = .5 + 3(.1) = 0.8 m ANSWER 1.2 to 2.8 m 2.0 ± 0.8 m ; full width 1.6 m .

words.definition: Position when the chosen interval begins.
An allowed range, not a standard deviation.
The ± value; full width is twice as large.
A condition treated as true, such as steady v .

title: Add the directions before the lengths
focus: Vector components, resultants, and direction angles
example: Two displacements are A = (6, −4) m and B = (−4, 8) m. Find their sum's magnitude and direction.
solution: GIVEN + x is east + y is north A and B use these axes. EQUATION Add x and y . Use the right triangle. WORK R = (2, 4) m | R | = √ 20 m θ = tan⁻¹(4/2) ANSWER 4.47 m 63.4° north of east .

words.definition: Signed part along an axis; keep axes fixed.
Sum: first tail to final tip.
Nonnegative size from perpendicular parts.
Both component signs locate the direction.

title: Negative acceleration does not always mean slowing
focus: Velocity changes, graph slopes, and a turning point
figure: COLOR IT · SLOW, THEN SPEED UP
example: A cart's velocity changes uniformly from +6 m/s to −2 m/s in 4 s . Find its acceleration and the time it reverses.
solution: GIVEN v i = +6 m/s v f = −2 m/s Δ t = 4 s EQUATION a = Δ v / Δ t . Turn: 0 = v i + at . WORK a = (−2 − 6)/4 0 = 6 − 2 t t = 3 s ANSWER a = −2 m/s² Slows for 3 s , then speeds up to the left.

words.definition: Change in velocity divided by elapsed time.
v and a have the same direction in 1D.
v and a oppose each other before the turn.
v = 0 for an instant; a can be nonzero.

title: Choose the equation that fits the information
focus: Constant acceleration, stopping distance, and independent checks
example: A car moving at +20 m/s brakes at −4 m/s² until it stops. Find its stopping distance, then check the result.
solution: GIVEN v i = +20 m/s v f = 0 m/s a = −4 m/s² EQUATION No time given: v f ² = v i ² + 2 a Δ x . WORK 0 = 400 − 8 Δ x t = (0 − 20)/(−4) area = ½(20)(5) ANSWER Δ x = +50 m 5 s to stop; area also gives 50 m .

words.definition: Equal velocity changes in equal times.
List supplied values before choosing.
Signed change in position, not distance.
Test with units, a graph or another equation.

title: Balanced forces can go with steady motion
focus: Newton's first law, inertia, and equilibrium
example: A cart is at −2 m , moving at +3 m/s . Its external forces balance for the next 4 s . Find its final position.
solution: GIVEN x 0 = −2 m v i = +3 m/s Σ F = 0; t = 4 s EQUATION First law: constant v . x f = x 0 + vt . WORK a = 0 m/s² x f = −2 + 3(4) ANSWER +10 m Net force zero; motion continues.

words.definition: An unforced object keeps its velocity.
Vector sum of external forces on a system.
More mass resists velocity change more.
Net force zero; v constant, not always zero.

title: Every force has a source and a receiver
focus: Weight, normal force, tension, and supported objects
figure: COLOR IT · ONE CRATE, THREE FORCES
example: A 3 kg crate rests on a table. A vertical rope pulls up with 10 N . Find the table's normal force. Use g = 9.8 N/kg .
solution: GIVEN m = 3 kg T = 10 N up a y = 0 EQUATION W = mg . N + T − W = 0. WORK W = 3(9.8) = 29.4 N N = 29.4 − 10 ANSWER N = 19.4 N The rope shares the support.

words.definition: Earth’s downward pull: mg .
Surface push, perpendicular to contact.
Rope’s pull along itself, away from the object.
The object a force acts on; also name its source.

title: The same force can produce different accelerations
focus: Total moving mass, inverse relationships, and experimental controls
example: Under the same net force, a 1 kg system accelerates at 4 m/s² and a 2 kg system at 2 m/s² . Predict a for a 3 kg system.
solution: GIVEN M 1 = 1 kg ; a 1 = 4 m/s² M 2 = 2 kg ; a 2 = 2 m/s² same net force EQUATION Check M × a . Then a = F net / M . WORK 1(4) = 2(2) = 4 N a 3 = 4 N ÷ 3 kg ANSWER 1.33 m/s² Assumes net force stays 4 N .

words.definition: All moving mass, including any hanger.
A value held fixed for a fair comparison.
Double M halves a at fixed net force.
Plot a against 1/ M to get an ideal line.

title: An applied pull is not always the net force
focus: Fixed mass, friction, and force-acceleration graphs
figure: COLOR IT · DRIVING VS. NET FORCE
example: A 2 kg system slides with 0.4 N of opposing friction. Compare acceleration with driving forces of 2 N and 4 N .
solution: GIVEN M = 2 kg f = 0.4 N F drive = 2 N , then 4 N EQUATION Subtract friction. Then a = F net / M . WORK a 1 = (2 − 0.4)/2 = 0.8 a 2 = (4 − 0.4)/2 = 1.8 ANSWER 0.8; 1.8 m/s² Driving force doubles; a does not.

words.definition: The pull before resistance is subtracted.
Driving force minus opposing resistance.
On an a -versus-net-force graph: 1/ M .
Fixed friction shifts the driving-force line down.

title: The force tells us how motion changes
focus: Net force, acceleration, and a cart moving the other way
example: A 4 kg cart has forces of 12 N right and 4 N left. Its initial velocity is −3 m/s . Find a and v after 1 s .
solution: GIVEN m = 4 kg F right = 12 N ; F left = 4 N v i = −3 m/s EQUATION Sum forces first. Σ F x = ma x . v = v i + a x t . WORK Σ F x = 12 − 4 = +8 N a x = 8/4 = +2 m/s² v = −3 + 2(1) ANSWER v = −1 m/s Still leftward; speed is now 1 m/s .

words.definition: Add signed forces along the same axis.
Velocity change from net force per mass.
Current motion; it can oppose a .
Opposite v and a : slows before reversal.

title: Equal forces can have unequal effects
focus: Newton's third law, separate objects, and system boundaries
example: Cart A has mass 1 kg ; cart B has mass 3 kg . Their interaction pushes A left and B right with 6 N each. Find both accelerations.
solution: GIVEN m A = 1 kg m B = 3 kg right is + EQUATION F = ma on each cart. No other horizontal forces. WORK a A = −6/1 = −6 m/s² a B = +6/3 = +2 m/s² ANSWER −6; +2 m/s² A has 3 times B’s acceleration size.

words.definition: A-on-B and B-on-A: equal and opposite.
Two objects; use separate force diagrams.
Same force size: smaller mass, larger a .
Pair forces cancel internally for combined A+B.

title: A force diagram begins with one chosen object
focus: External interactions, scaled arrows, and an accelerating lamp
example: A rope lifts a 2 kg lamp with upward acceleration 1.5 m/s² . Find the tension. Use g = 9.8 m/s² .
solution: GIVEN m = 2 kg a y = +1.5 m/s² g = 9.8 m/s² EQUATION Up is +. T − mg = ma y . WORK W = 2(9.8) = 19.6 N T = 19.6 + 2(1.5) ANSWER T = 22.6 N T and W are not a third-law pair.

words.definition: The receiver of every force in the diagram.
A force from outside the chosen boundary.
Use one scale to show each force’s size.
Sum of forces, not another interaction.

title: Choose axes that help explain the ramp
focus: Inclined surfaces, weight components, and normal force
example: A 2 kg block slides down a 30° ramp with 2 N friction uphill. Find its acceleration and normal force. Use g = 9.8 m/s² .
solution: GIVEN m = 2 kg ; θ = 30° f = 2 N uphill a ⊥ = 0 EQUATION mg sin θ − f = ma ∥ N = mg cos θ WORK a ∥ = [19.6(0.5) − 2]/2 N = 19.6 cos 30° ANSWER 3.9 m/s² Downhill; N ≈ 17.0 N .

words.definition: Along the ramp; choose downhill as +.
Straight out of the ramp, usually not vertical.
mg sin θ along; mg cos θ into the ramp.
No motion through the surface: a ⊥ = 0.

title: Friction changes when slipping begins
focus: Adjustable static friction and the kinetic-friction model
figure: COLOR IT · BEFORE AND AFTER SLIP
example: For this box, compare a 6 N pull while at rest with a 10 N pull after sliding starts. Use g = 9.8 m/s² ; pulls are horizontal.
solution: GIVEN N = 2(9.8) = 19.6 N μ s = 0.40 μ k = 0.25 EQUATION Check μ s N . Sliding: use μ k N , then net force. WORK f s ,max = 7.84 N at rest: f s = 6 N a = (10 − 4.9)/2 ANSWER 0; 2.55 m/s² At rest, then sliding.

words.definition: Adjusts to prevent slip, up to a limit.
f s ,max = μ s N ; f s can be smaller.
Opposes sliding; model size μ k N .
Find the perpendicular force balance first.

title: Balance each direction, not just the force sizes
focus: Equilibrium, angled ropes, and component sums
example: A 40 N sign hangs at rest from two equal ropes, each 30° above horizontal. Find the tension in each rope.
solution: GIVEN W = 40 N ; θ = 30° equal tensions a = 0 EQUATION x parts cancel. 2 T sin 30° = 40 N . WORK 2 T (0.5) = 40 N T = 40 N ANSWER 40 N per rope Each rope gives 20 N upward.

words.definition: Zero a : forces sum to zero on each axis.
Vertical parts support the weight.
Equal angles and loading: equal tensions.
v = 0 alone does not prove balance.

title: Find the first step that changes the story
focus: Repairing force sums, signs, and interpretations
figure: COLOR IT · CHECK THE CHANGE IN v
example: A 3 kg cart has 9 N right and 3 N left. Someone writes a = 9/3 = 3 m/s² . Explain and repair the first wrong step.
solution: GIVEN m = 3 kg right is + forces: +9 N and −3 N EQUATION Use net force, not the largest force. WORK Σ F x = 9 − 3 = +6 N a x = 6/3 = +2 m/s² ANSWER +2 m/s² Check: ma = 6 N .

words.definition: Name what is found: position, speed, etc.
Direction uses signs; speed is a size.
Sum all forces on the same object.
Use a graph or another equation.

title: Follow the chain from force to position
focus: Constant net force, velocity reversal, and signed displacement
example: A 2 kg cart starts at 1 m with velocity −2 m/s . A constant +4 N net force acts for 3 s . Find final velocity and position.
solution: GIVEN m = 2 kg ; Σ F = +4 N x 0 = 1 m ; v i = −2 m/s t = 3 s EQUATION Find a from force. Then steady-a equations. WORK a = 4/2 = +2 m/s² v f = −2 + 2(3) x f = 1 − 6 + 9 ANSWER +4 m/s ; +4 m Δ x = +3 m ; distance = 5 m .

words.definition: Net force → a → velocity and position.
Keep one start and end time throughout.
v can cross zero while a keeps its sign.
Add positive and negative pieces of Δ x .

title: Build a prediction one coordinate at a time
focus: A two-dimensional plan with fixed axes and clear assumptions
example: A probe starts at (−20, 5) m and moves at 10 m/s , 30° from + x toward + y , for 2 s . Find its new coordinates.
solution: GIVEN x 0 = −20 m ; y 0 = 5 m v = 10 m/s ; θ = 30° t = 2 s ; steady v EQUATION Resolve v : v x = 8.66 m/s v y = 5 m/s WORK x f = −20 + 8.66(2) y f = 5 + 5(2) ANSWER (−2.68, 15) m Final x is still negative.

words.definition: Keep the origin and axes fixed.
Signed x and y parts; calculate separately.
Make all units match before substituting.
State assumptions, such as steady velocity.

title: A good forecast can change with the evidence
focus: Defending a claim, comparing ranges, and explaining revision
example: Keep x 0 = 8 ± 0.5 m and exact t = 3 s . A new measurement changes v from −2.0 to −1.5 ± 0.1 m/s . Update the forecast.
solution: GIVEN x 0 = 8 ± 0.5 m v = −1.5 ± 0.1 m/s exact t = 3 s EQUATION Update center and conservative bound. WORK x f = 8 − 1.5(3) δ x = .5 + 3(.1) = 0.8 m ANSWER 2.7 to 4.3 m Center shifts +1.5 m .

words.definition: Result, units, time, direction and range.
A measurement or calculation supporting a step.
An uncertain input or missing effect.
Name the change and show its effect.
